card.hook: From the Bund, the Lujiazui skyline lines up across the river like a team photo, and Shanghai Tower is the tallest one in it. It's the classic postcard view, and it's easy to get.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Bund waterfront (外滩) on the west bank, near the Meteorological Signal Tower on Zhongshan East 1st Road. Face across the Huangpu River: Shanghai Tower is to the north-east, with the other Lujiazui towers lined up beside it. Most people shoot from the stone barrier at water level, so arrive a little early for a clear spot at the railing.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the river and the whole row of towers. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull Shanghai Tower closer, or 0.5x if you want lots of waterfront and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tower on a vertical line and let the river fill the bottom third, so the tower stands straight and the picture has depth.
card.best_time: Aim for about 20 to 40 minutes after sunset, when the sky still has some colour and the towers are lit. Haze can dull the view, so clear weather is best.
card.selfie_here: Try the street crossing of Dongtai Road and Huayuan Shiqiao Road (东台路与花园石桥路) in Lujiazui. One guide calls it roughly the centre of the three towers, so they can rise behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and angle it up. This is a close match rather than a guaranteed tower-behind-you spot, so check what's in your frame.
card.ask_someone: For a full-length shot, ask a passer-by on the sidewalk outside Lujiazui Metro Exit 9A, directly north of the tower, to shoot upward with you standing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The Bund waterfront is an open public street and walkway. The 118th-floor deck allows non-professional photo gear, so your phone is fine up there.
card.challenge: Keep the tower perfectly straight and fit a strip of river along the bottom, with no leaning tower of Pudong allowed.
card.good_to_know: Shanghai Tower is the tallest building in China, at 128 storeys and 632 metres. It's the tallest of a trio with the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center, a grouping planners drew up back in 1993. Building began in November 2008 and it topped out in 2013. The 118th and 119th floor decks have been fully open since April 2017, and "Top of Shanghai" on the 121st floor (562 metres) came later.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Bund waterfront (外滩) on the west bank, near the Meteorological Signal Tower on Zhongshan East 1st Road. Face across the Huangpu River: Shanghai Tower is to the north-east, with the other Lujiazui towers lined up beside it. Most people shoot from the stone barrier at water level, so arrive a little early for a clear spot at the railing.

card.hook: Grey-tiled dragon walls ripple along their wavy ridges, a rockery 12 metres tall rises behind them, and a zigzag bridge is just outside. Yu Garden packs about 2 hectares with so many photo ideas that you'll be snapping before you've found your bearings.
card.stand_here: Stand about 55 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near 积玉水廊, and face north-west. The middle of the garden is about a minute's walk that way.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole scene of roofs, walls and water. Drop to 0.5x in tight courtyards, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof ridges and carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and set a roofline or dragon-wall ridge along one of the horizontal lines, with a bit of water or a bridge in front for depth.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, and soft light or gentle overcast suits the grey tiles. In the evening, when the lanterns and lights come on, switch to night mode.
card.selfie_here: Try the Nine-Turn Bridge (Jiuqu Bridge): stand on the zigzag bridge over the pond with the bazaar's pavilions and traditional buildings behind you, and use the front camera at arm's length. For something quieter, step into one of the round moon gates by the bamboo grove beside Heralding Spring Hall and let the garden frame you like a painting.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the little pond at the foot of the Grand Rockery and shoot upward, so the whole rock formation fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the garden and bazaar. Selfie sticks are banned at almost all Chinese heritage sites, so leave yours behind. Stay on the paths and don't climb on rocks or walls. Check the official site for what's open and how entry works.
card.challenge: Find a roof corner that curls up like it's waving at the sky, then get one wide shot and one close-up of it from the same spot.
card.good_to_know: Pan Yunduan began the garden in 1559, in the Ming dynasty, as a comfort for his father in old age. Work was held up for years and it was finished in 1577. It opened to the public in 1961 and became a national monument in 1982.

card.hook: Picture old stone banks on your left, a wide brown river in the middle and glass towers on your right, all in one phone shot. That's the Bund, and it's the reason half of Shanghai's holiday photos look alike (in a good way).
card.stand_here: Stand in 陈毅广场 (Chen Yi Square), in the middle of the Bund promenade near Bund 9–12, at the river railing. Face the river and you get the colonial facades at the left edge, the river in the centre and Pudong on the right.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic river-and-skyline view. Switch to 0.5x if the crowd is close and you want the facades, river and towers all in one frame. Try zoom 2x or 5x to pick out the Pudong towers or a single facade detail (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the river on the lower third, keep the skyline level, and tap the sky then drag the slider a touch darker so the lit buildings don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, when the facades and towers glow against a darkening sky. Arrive early to bag a spot at the railing. The Bund's lights are reported to go off around 22:00 and light-show schedules can change, so don't leave it late.
card.selfie_here: Squeeze in at the railing in front of the Chen Yi statue, or stand on the promenade opposite Bund 12 (the old HSBC Building). Use the front camera at 0.5x so the river and the Pudong skyline fill the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the old facades behind you, cross to the Lujiazui riverside path north of the Oriental Pearl Tower, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame you with the Bund's buildings across the water.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are banned in central Shanghai, including the Bund. Crowds, events and rules can change, so check the official site before you go. Pickpocketing is rare but not unheard of on packed weekend nights, so keep your phone in a front pocket between shots.
card.challenge: Get the facades, the river and the towers in one shot with no stranger's head sneaking in. Bonus points if you do it on a busy evening.
card.good_to_know: The Bund runs about 1.6 km from Yan'an Road to Waibaidu Bridge, with some 52 buildings in Neoclassical, Gothic, Art Deco and other styles. Some echo the waterfront of Liverpool. After typhoon floods the embankment was raised about 10 metres above street level, and the widened promenade reopened in March 2010.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in 陈毅广场 (Chen Yi Square), in the middle of the Bund promenade near Bund 9–12, at the river railing. Face the river and you get the colonial facades at the left edge, the river in the centre and Pudong on the right.

card.hook: There's a giant shiny metal egg by the river, and right behind it Shanghai's pink-and-silver spaceship is parked on the skyline. It's a much calmer spot than the busy Bund, so you can take your time.
card.stand_here: Stand in North Bund Greenland, on the waterfront near the metal egg-shaped restaurant. Walk to the river edge and face south: the tower is straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the egg and the tower both fit. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot, and use 0.5x only when you want a big, dramatic egg up front.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the tower's lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Come for sunset and stay into the blue hour just after, when the tower's lights come on against a deep blue sky. The lighting runs into the late evening, so there's no rush to leave.
card.selfie_here: Head across to the front of The Ritz-Carlton Shanghai in Pudong (Lujiazui) and stand in front of the hotel building with the tower directly behind you. Use your front camera, switch to 0.5x if it has one, and let the tower rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk toward the Shanghai Port International Cruise Terminal, find the slope leading out of the parking lot, and ask someone to stand at the foot of it and shoot upward so the tower fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are banned throughout the Lujiazui area, and security will confiscate them if they spot one.
card.challenge: Put the egg low in the frame, the tower on a gridline, and take three shots with different amounts of sky. Then pick your winner like a very serious judge.
card.good_to_know: The Oriental Pearl Tower was built between 1991 and 1994 and stands 468 metres tall with its antenna. It was the tallest structure in China until 2007. Its spheres are covered in red glass and concrete tiles, which is why you can spot it from so far away.

card.hook: Skip the rush to the neon and start at the bronze monument by People's Square, because it's the street's own welcome sign. Take this shot first, then wander off and get lost in the shops.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street bronze monument, near People's Square Metro Exit 19 at the west end of the pedestrian street. It's a separate stop from the subject, which is about 690 metres to the north-east. Stand just west of the monument and face east, so the street stretches away behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the monument with the street behind it. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze in the full width of the street. Later, try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out signs and the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the monument on one third of the frame, then crouch a little so it stands out against the buildings.
card.best_time: Dusk and evening look best. The neon usually comes on around 6 pm in winter or 7 pm in summer and runs until about 10 pm. Weekdays are quieter, because weekend crowds are heavy.
card.selfie_here: Try the bronze monument by Exit 19: it carries the street's own name, so your selfie shows the landmark right behind you. Or go to the Bund end by the Peace Hotel, where the pedestrian street starts beside the river and runs west behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the monument or street over your shoulder. Both are good bets rather than official photo points.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed on Nanjing Road, but be mindful of private businesses and don't photograph individuals intrusively without their consent. Watch for pickpockets in crowded zones while you hunt for an angle, and check the official site before you go for any events or temporary closures.
card.challenge: Get the monument on one third of your frame, crouch, and see how many shop signs you can fit in the street behind it without losing the monument.
card.good_to_know: The road dates back to 1845, when it was called Park Lane, and it became Nanking Road in 1862. Early in the 20th century eight big department stores opened along it, and some of the older ones are still here. In 2019–2020 the pedestrian zone was extended east towards the Bund.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: the best view of Xintiandi's old grey-brick rooftops is from the park next door, across a still lake that doubles them in the water. Modern towers peek over the top, so old and new land in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in 太平湖, east of the Xintiandi lanes, on the lake shore inside Taipingqiao Park. Stand at the water's edge and face the shikumen rooftops across the lake.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lake, the rooftops and the towers together. Tap 2x or more to pick out the grey-brick roofs and leave the foreground out. In the narrow lanes, switch to zoom 0.5x for a long view of the frontages.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the waterline on a lower third line, so the rooftops and their reflection fill the frame and the towers stay straight.
card.best_time: Dusk is the one to aim for at the lake, when the fountain lights come on. Weekend midday is the busiest time, so a weekday or an earlier hour gives you fewer people in your pictures.
card.selfie_here: Try the entrance to one of the shikumen lanes, with the old stone-framed gateway behind you, which one guide calls the best photo spot. The cobblestone alleys of the North Block, lined with stone gate houses, are another good pick. Use your front camera and keep the gateway over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: In the plum-rain season (June to early July) the stone lanes can be slippery, so watch your footing while you frame a shot. Ask before photographing inside shops and restaurants.
card.challenge: Take the same rooftop shot twice, once with the reflection and once with only the real roofs, then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: Xintiandi is a car-free district of shopping, cafés and restaurants in the former French Concession. It is built around rebuilt shikumen ("stone gate") houses, and the redevelopment was completed in 2001. For second shots, walk the stone-gated frontages along 马当路 for a long view of gateways receding, or the narrow 新天地北里 for a tighter frame.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in 太平湖, east of the Xintiandi lanes, on the lake shore inside Taipingqiao Park. Stand at the water's edge and face the shikumen rooftops across the lake.

card.hook: Gold roofs, a pagoda, and a wall of glass office towers all squeezed into one frame, with a Metro entrance up front to prove you're in the middle of the city. Jing'an Temple is old meets new, and your phone loves it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the north-side pavement of 南京西路 (West Nanjing Road), directly across the road from the temple. Face south, so the golden roofs and pagoda sit in front of the towers.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the roofs, pagoda and towers all in one shot. Then try 2x to bring the gold roofs closer and stack the towers behind them. Use 0.5x only if you want the whole street, and watch for stretched edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gold roof, then drag the slider down a little to make it darker, so the gold keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the hour before sunset, when warm light hits the gold roofs and the glass towers sit in shadow. Lighting at night varies, so check the schedule before you go if you want to see the temple lit up.
card.selfie_here: Try Jing'an Temple Plaza: step a little away from the entrance flow and use the front camera with the guardian lions or the roofline behind you. Or go to the pool outside Exit 14 of Jing'an Temple Station, and when the water is still, hold your phone low so the golden roof and its reflection both appear over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the north-side pavement of West Nanjing Road facing south, while you stand in front of the temple so the roofs, pagoda and towers all fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: On the Huashan Road / Yan'an West Road pedestrian overpass, don't climb the railing or block other pedestrians. You can photograph the outside from the pavement without a ticket, but the temple itself is a place of worship, so check the official site for entry and opening hours.
card.challenge: Take one shot at 1x and one at 2x from the same spot, then pick the winner. Bonus points if the Metro entrance is clear of people.
card.good_to_know: The temple's name means 'Temple of Peace and Tranquility'. The first temple on an earlier site dates back to 247 AD, and it moved to its present spot in 1216. It was razed in the Cultural Revolution and rebuilt from 1983, and the Jing'an Pagoda was completed in 2010, so most of what you see is recent, built on a very old foundation.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the north-side pavement of 南京西路 (West Nanjing Road), directly across the road from the temple. Face south, so the golden roofs and pagoda sit in front of the towers.

card.hook: Look up the second you step in: electricity cables sag overhead and air-conditioning units cling to the walls like barnacles. Tianzifang still feels lived-in, and that's exactly why it's fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Walk north to 泰康路210弄, the Taikang Road entrance, and stand just outside and under the stone gate. Face the gate so you can see the Tianzifang stele above it and the first narrow shikumen lane running back into the alley.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole stone gate and the stele into one frame. Switch to 1x for the lane itself, then 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for lanterns, signs and carved doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up with the centre line so the lane leads the eye, then tap the brightest part of the gate or sky and slide it a little darker to keep the stonework detail.
card.best_time: Go earlier in the day when the lanes are quieter, so you can shoot the gate without a crowd in it. Soft daylight is kind to the stonework and the shaded lanes.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Lane 210 entrance on Taikang Road, under the stone arch of the shikumen gate. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the arch, the sky and the lane behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Lane 210 entrance and shoot slightly upwards while you stand under the stone arch, with the lane and sky behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Many people live here, so keep your phone out of open doorways and off residents' front steps. Ask permission before taking close-ups of people or photos inside private shops. The lanes are narrow, so step aside when you stop to shoot.
card.challenge: Find a cross-alley, hold your phone high, point it straight up, and see how many of these you can fit in one shot: wires, washing and a lantern.
card.good_to_know: Tianzifang grew out of a shikumen housing estate built in 1933, in the old French Concession area of Shanghai. Today it holds more than 200 small businesses, including cafés, galleries, craft shops and studios. Shop fronts and signs may have changed, so check on the day.

card.hook: Picture a giant ancient bronze cooking pot sitting on a city square. That's the Shanghai Museum, and the building is the star of your photo.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, which sits right at the Shanghai Museum on People's Square. Then walk away from the building, facing it, until the round top and square base both fit in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from a few steps back to catch the whole building. Use zoom 0.5x only if you can't step back far enough. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a close shot of the rounded top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the square base up with them, so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Visitors say People's Square looks best at golden hour, so aim for that if you can. If you're shooting after dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Out on the square there's a big seasonal tulip garden, which a travel blog suggests as a check-in spot after you leave the museum. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and step back so the museum fits over your shoulder. That blog doesn't say the museum shows behind you, so check your screen before you smile.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash photography is generally prohibited, and photos may only be allowed in certain galleries. Selfie sticks are banned in some galleries too. Check the official site before you go in for entry details and photo rules.
card.challenge: Fit the round top and the square base in one frame, then see if you can spot 'round sky, square earth' in your shot.
card.good_to_know: Architect Xing Tonghe shaped the building like a ding, an ancient bronze cooking vessel. The round top and square base stand for the old idea of 'round sky, square earth'. The museum was founded in 1952 and moved into this building on 12 October 1996. It's 29.5 metres high with five floors, and it holds more than 120,000 pieces.

card.hook: Look for the pale green pointy roof. It's copper that has weathered to green, it's about 10 metres tall, and it's the easiest thing on the Bund to spot.

card.best_time: Get there before 6:30 PM to snag a front-row spot. Around 18:00 or after 22:00 is a good time for the Bund view, and the promenade is busiest between 7 and 9 PM.

card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is being renovated until 2027 but stays open, so the building may look a bit different when you arrive. The promenade is open to everyone, but the interiors and rooftop terrace are reached through the hotel, so check the official site first.

card.hook: You'll end up with your head tipped right back, staring up at a skyscraper with a giant hole near the top. Locals call it "the bottle opener", and once you've seen it you can't unsee it.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze all three towers into one frame, since you're so close. Switch to 1x for a tidier shot of the World Financial Center on its own, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the opening at the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up one straight edge of the tower with a grid line, then tilt the phone up only as far as you need so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Dusk is worth trying, when the sky still has some colour and the building lights are on. In the daytime, a clear sky gives you the cleanest edges. After dark, use night mode and keep your elbows tucked in to your body.
card.selfie_here: Try the Lujiazui Riverside Promenade, where you get an up-close view of the three towers. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the towers over your shoulder, and check the framing when you get there.
card.ask_someone: For a full skyline shot of you, stand on Waibaidu Bridge (over Suzhou Creek, near Huangpu Lu) with the Pudong skyline across the water, and ask a passer-by to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck has closed for good, so this is a view from the outside only. Access around the rear ramp may change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the bottle opener, all three towers and a perfectly straight edge lined up on a grid line in one shot?
card.good_to_know: The tower is 492 metres tall and was designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox. The opening near the top replaced an earlier circular design that drew objections. It topped out in September 2007 and opened in August 2008. With the Shanghai Tower and Jin Mao Tower, it forms the first group of three supertall buildings standing side by side.

card.hook: Picture a fountain in the foreground, a wide green lawn behind it, and a ring of towers and cultural buildings closing in around the edges. That's People's Square, right in the middle of Shanghai, and it's a friendly place to start your city photos.
card.stand_here: Stand in 人民广场 (the central plaza), right by the fountain. Face across the water towards the lawn and the buildings around the square. The rest of the square lies to the south-east of this spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the fountain, lawn and buildings all fit in one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out building details or the fountain's jets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on the lower third and crouch a little so the water sits against the skyline.
card.best_time: Evening, when the fountain is lit up. In the daytime it runs on a schedule, so check the timings on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try People's Park, the green space right next to the square. No single corner is named, so just pick a leafy spot. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more greenery, and hold your arm a bit higher.
card.rules_and_safety: Leave the selfie stick at the hotel or in a locker, as they're almost always banned in Chinese museums, including the Shanghai Museum on the square. The weekend marriage market is a place to be discreet, so ask before photographing individuals. The museums and the Urban Planning Exhibition Hall have their own entry rules, so check the official site. Watch for wet ground and any safety notices outdoors.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the fountain's water seems to touch the skyline, then take one more from a crouch and see which you like better.
card.good_to_know: Before 1949 this was a horse-racing course owned by the Shanghai Race Club. In the 1990s the city government headquarters and the Shanghai Museum moved in. The old clubhouse became the Shanghai Art Museum, and part of the track became People's Park next door.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in 人民广场 (the central plaza), right by the fountain. Face across the water towards the lawn and the buildings around the square. The rest of the square lies to the south-east of this spot.

card.hook: Jin Mao is the skyscraper that looks like it's wearing a stack of pagoda roofs. Your eye climbs the ledges one by one, and that's why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand on 外滩 (The Bund), on the west bank promenade on Zhongshan East 1st Road. Face across the Huangpu towards Pudong and look for Jin Mao in the Lujiazui skyline, with the historic Bund buildings in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole skyline with the Bund facades in the foreground. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the stepped upper tiers. If you ever get right up close, 0.5x lets you tilt up and fit much more of the tower in.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or a mid-tone part of the tower, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the glass doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good bet, when the sky is softer and the glass picks up its colour. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the shot steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the open garden space at the IFC Mall sky garden in Lujiazui, with Jin Mao rising behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and tilt up so the stepped tower stays over your shoulder. The park at Lujiazui Central Green also works, because Jin Mao shows up there alongside the other two supertall towers.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the intersection of Dongtai Road and Huayuan Shiqiao Road in Lujiazui, and ask them to step back so all three towers, Jin Mao included, fit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The outdoor Skywalk is ticketed, and you can't take your own phone onto it. Staff take the photos, and you'll be fitted with a safety harness. The hotel has its own entrance, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: The tower has 16 segments, each a bit shorter than the one below, so try counting them in your photo.
card.good_to_know: Jin Mao rises 420.5 metres over 88 floors and was dedicated on 28 August 1998, a date picked because 8 is a lucky number in Chinese culture. The stepped outline is meant to recall a tiered pagoda. The Grand Hyatt takes the upper floors from the 53rd up, and the indoor Skywalk observation deck is on the 88th floor.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on 外滩 (The Bund), on the west bank promenade on Zhongshan East 1st Road. Face across the Huangpu towards Pudong and look for Jin Mao in the Lujiazui skyline, with the historic Bund buildings in front of you.

card.hook: Most people rush through the gate to find the jade statues, but the best shot is waiting on the street. A glowing yellow wall with a curved roofline floating above it, and you haven't even bought a ticket yet.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Anyuan Road pavement outside the temple and face the ornate yellow front wall. The phone icon sits in the middle of the temple, so use it to find the place, then head to the frontage for this shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole long wall and roofline in from the pavement. Try 1x for a more natural look, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the wall up with a horizontal line so it doesn't lean, and keep the curved roofline near the top third.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, in the morning or late afternoon. Check the official site for current opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the temple courtyard inside the grounds: use the front camera and stand with the traditional buildings behind you. Late afternoon is lovely there, when warm light filters through the trees.
card.rules_and_safety: No photos inside the Jade Buddha Chamber, and rules vary from hall to hall, so follow the posted signs. Courtyards and outdoor areas are fine for photos. Ask before photographing monks or worshippers, don't photograph ceremonies, and skip the flash and keep your phone on silent.

card.hook: Picture a zigzag bridge, a pond full of glowing lantern reflections and a stack of upturned roofs, all in a busy pedestrian zone full of shops and restaurants. That's the City God Temple scene, and it looks best once the sun goes down.
card.stand_here: Walk onto 九曲桥, the zigzag bridge, and stop in the middle, facing the lake. The pond and bridge sit just north-west of the temple buildings, and from here you get the bridge in front, the Huxinting pavilion over the water and the temple roofs behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge, pavilion and roofs together. If the bridge is packed and you can't fit it all in, tap zoom 0.5x. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved eaves and roof ridges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and let the zigzag rail lead your eye to the pavilion, with the roofs filling the top of the frame and the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go after dusk, when the lanterns come on and the pond picks up their reflections. One guide suggests roughly 18:30 to 19:30. Weekends and holidays are the busiest, so be patient and wait for a gap rather than fighting for the exact centre of the bridge.
card.selfie_here: Try the Dragon Wall in the inner courtyards of the temple, near the carved stone dragon head. A traveller tip says it makes for historic-looking photos. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the dragon behind your shoulder. It's worth double-checking the exact spot when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the stone lions at the main entrance and ask someone to shoot upward so the eaves fill the frame above you, which also helps avoid the crowds.
card.rules_and_safety: The temple itself is a ticketed place of worship, so check the official site for entry and opening times. Photographing the deities inside the halls isn't allowed. Photography is generally fine in public areas, but be discreet and respectful, especially around people praying.
card.challenge: Can you get the zigzag rail, the pavilion and at least three lantern reflections in one shot without a single stranger's head in it?
card.good_to_know: The temple began as a shrine to the spirit of Jinshan, an island off the coast, and became a City God Temple in 1403. It honours three protectors of the city: a Han dynasty chancellor, a Ming-era official and a Qing general who died defending Shanghai in the First Opium War. It was closed during the Cultural Revolution, then fully restored in 2005-06 and reopened in October 2006.

card.selfie_here: Try the check-in spot just outside Gate 1 on Beijing West Road, where the park's Kawazu cherry blossoms bloom in season. card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks may be restricted inside the museum, and flash may be restricted near delicate exhibits, so look for signs. Check opening and entry details locally before you go.
card.challenge: Find something in the park, like a path or a plant, to put in the foreground, and see if you can make the building look even bigger.
card.good_to_know: The Shanghai Natural History Museum opened at this site in Jing'an Sculpture Park in 2015, in a purpose-built building of 44,517 square metres. The museum itself began in 1956 in the old Shanghai Cotton Exchange Building on East Yan'an Road, so this is its newer home. Inside are about 240,000 samples, including a 140-million-year-old Mamenchisaurus skeleton over four storeys high, a giant panda and a Yellow River mammoth.

card.hook: Most bridges just get you across the water. This one is a giant dark steel frame with a skyline tucked behind it, and the criss-crossing ironwork does half the composing for you.

card.good_to_know: Waibaidu Bridge, also called the Garden Bridge, is the first all-steel bridge in China. It's also the only surviving camelback truss bridge there. It opened on 20 January 1908 as the fourth Western-designed bridge on this spot since 1856, and was declared Heritage Architecture in 1994.
